trascrizione: You are at the Gallerie de l'Academia, the museum that holds the largest collection of Venetian painting in the world,
five centuries of art, from the 14th to the 18th century, gathered in one place.
The museum was born at the beginning of the 19th century, but its story starts earlier.
In 1750 the Republic founded an Academy of Fine Arts, a school for painters and sculptors.
A few decades later, with the fall of the Republic and the suppressions ordered by
Napoleon, many churches, convents and confraternities were closed, and their paintings risked being lost or scattered.
Many were brought here, and in 1817 the gallery opened to the public.
The museum occupies three historic buildings, the church of Santamaria della Curita,
the squalor grande of the same name, and a convent partly designed by Andréa Palladio.
This is why some works are still in the very place for which they were created.
Begin in the first room, the great chapter hall of the Squalor della Curita.
Look up at the gilded wooden ceiling, full of carved angels.
Beneath it hang polyptics from the 14th and early 15th centuries, with their gold backgrounds,
such as those by Paolo Veneziano.
This is the starting point of Venetian painting, still close to the Byzantine world.
Moving on, you meet the great Renaissance altarpieces,
including Giovanni Bellini's San Giobe altarpiece, the Virgin enthroned,
the saints around her, and three music-making angels at her feet,
within a painted architecture that seems to continue the real architecture of the church it was made for.
Then comes one of the most mysterious works in the history of art,
Giorgione's Tempest.
A young woman, nurses a child, a man stands watching her,
and in the background a flash of lightning tears across the sky above a city.
What does it represent?
No one knows for sure, and scholars have debated it for centuries.
Perhaps that is precisely its charm.
Further on are the great Tilleri, the huge canvases that decorated the halls of the Venetian Squalor.
From San Giovanni Evangelista come the miracles of the cross,
with Gentia Bellini's procession in St Mark's Square,
and Carpaccio's view of the old wooden Rialto Bridge.
Carpaccio also painted the cycle of Saint Ursula, the Breton Princess who sets off on pilgrimage
with 11,000 virgins, a long story told like a serialized novel, full of ships,
cities and details of everyday life.
Then stop in front of a gigantic canvas by Paolo Veroneze.
It was meant to be a last supper, but the painter filled it with figures that had
nothing sacred about them, soldiers, servants, gestures, even dogs and a parrot.
In 1573, the Inquisition summoned him and asked him to correct it.
Veroneze found a solution.
Instead of changing the painting, he changed the title.
Since then it has been called the Feast in the House of Levi.
Look also for Tintoretto's miracle of the slave, the work that made him famous in 1548.
Saint Mark plunges down from the sky headfirst to save a condemned slave,
with a movement that left Venetians open-mouthed.
Towards the end of the route is Titian's last painting, the Pieta.
The painter worked on it as a very old man during the plague of 1576,
perhaps thinking of his own tomb, but he died before finishing it.
It was completed by a pupil, Palma Ilgevane.
The painter's applied almost with the fingers in a free and dramatic way.
The four leaving don't overlook the 18th century,
the last great age of Venetian painting.
Here you will find the pastel portraits of Rosalba Carriera,
one of the most celebrated painters in Europe in her day,
sought after by kings and princes, the luminous works of Giambattista Tiappolo,
and an architectural capriccio by Canaletto,
the painting he presented to the academy itself, to be admitted as a member.
Finally in the alburgo room of the Squola della Carita,
you can see a work that has remained exactly where it was painted,
Titian's presentation of the Virgin in the temple.
The young Mary climbs a great staircase on her own,
while below, an old woman selling eggs watches the scene, unconcerned.
A curiosity, the gallery also owned Leonardo da Vinci's famous Vitruvian man.
To protect it from light however, it is put on display only rarely.
As you leave you will find yourself in front of the academia bridge,
one of the four bridges over the Grand Canal.
From the bridge, look towards the Basilica della Salute.
It is one of the most famous views in Venice,
and you have probably already seen it in many paintings.
Before you, overlooking the Grand Canal, stands the Cadoro, considered the most beautiful
Gothic Palace in Venice.
Its finest façade is seen from the water, but even from the alley leading to the entrance
you can sense how special it is.
The palace was built between 1421 and 1440 for Marino Contorini, a wealthy Venetian
merchant and nobleman who wanted a home that would amaze the whole city.
He called on the best stone masons of the time, including Giovanni and Bartolomeo Bonn,
the same masters who created the Porta Delicata of the Doge's Palace.
The name, the House of Gold, comes from how the façade originally looked.
The stone decorations were painted in precious colors, such as ultramarine blue and
vermilion red, and many details were covered in gold leaf.
The sunlight reflected from the canal made the whole façade shine.
Today the golden colors have almost disappeared, but the name has remained.
Look at the façade if you can, from the water bus or from the opposite bank.
It is asymmetrical.
On one side the lodges open one above the other, as light as lace made of stone.
On the other is a more solid wall, decorated with marble panels.
Along the top runs a slender white crenellation that looks as if it were made of lace.
Like many Venetian palaces, the Cadoro was both a home and a place of business.
On the ground floor, open to the water, goods were unloaded and stored.
On the upper floors were the family's rooms, arranged around the Portego,
the great hall running right through the building from the canal to the courtyard.
Over the following centuries the palace passed from owner to owner and was altered several times.
In the 19th century it was bought by the famous ballerina Maria Taleoni, who had it altered with little respect.
The outdoor staircase in the courtyard was removed and the splendid red stone wellhead was sold.
Salvation came in 1894 when the palace was bought by Baron Giorgio Franchetti, a passionate art collector.
Franchetti devoted the rest of his life to restoring it.
He bought back the wellhead, carved in the 15th century by Bartolomeo Bonn, with the figures of charity, justice and fortitude,
rebuilt the courtyard and laid part of the mosaic floor with his own hands, inspired by the floors of Venice's ancient churches.
In 1916 he gave the palace and his collection to the state, so that it could become a museum open to all,
and he wished his ashes to remain here.
Today the Cadoro houses the Giorgio Franchetti Gallery.
Its most famous work is Andeo Mantegna's San Sebastian, placed in a small chapel that Franchetti created especially for it.
The saint, pierced by arrows, seems almost a step out of the niche.
At his feet a Latin scroll reminds us that only what is divine is eternal and everything else is smoke.
The museum also holds paintings by Carpaccio, Titian and many other Venetian artists, sculptures, small bronzes,
and some fragments of the frescoes by Giorgio Neantitian that once decorated the façade of the Fondacó de Tedeschi, near the Rialto Bridge.
Before leaving, step out onto the loggio overlooking the Grand Canal.
From here you can watch the boats go by, the Rialto Market on the opposite bank and the life of the city.
The same view Marino Contorini wanted to enjoy from his house of gold almost 600 years ago.
Hidden in a small courtyard, a few steps from Campo Manin is one of the most surprising
pieces of architecture in Venice, the Scala Contorini del Bovolo.
The name comes from its shape.
In Venetian, Bovolo means snail, and one look is enough to see why the staircase spirals
up inside a cylindrical tower, opening to the outside through a series of white arches
that wind around themselves, like a snail's shell.
The staircase was built at the end of the 15th century for the Contorini, one of the most
powerful families of the Republic.
The palace was small and the courtyard narrow, and the Contorini wanted an elegant link between
the floors but also something that would get people talking about them.
The result was so original that this branch of the family took the name Contorini del
Bovolo.
The staircase is attributed to Giovanni Candi, a little known master builder who created
his masterpiece here.
Notice the style.
It combines gothic and early Renaissance elements, with slender arches, small columns and balustrades
in white Istrian stone that stand out against the red brick of the tower.
If you climb the steps, you reach the Belvedere at the top.
From up there an extraordinary view opens over the rooftops of Venice, the bell towers
and the dome of St. Mark's Basilica, not far away.
The staircase has also attracted filmmakers.
Orson Welles chose it as the setting for some scenes of his Othello, shot in Venice in the
early 1950s.
After a long restoration, the staircase reopened to the public in 2016.
Stop for a moment in the courtyard and watch the spiral rising towards the sky.
It is one of those places you discover almost by chance, and which make Venice
a city full of surprises.
Before you on the island of the Giudecca rises the Church of the Redentor, one of Andrea
Palladio's masterpieces.
With its great white dome and luminous façade it is reflected in the wide canal that separates
it from the Zata.
Like the Basilica della Salute, this church was born of a promise.
Between 1575 and 1577 a terrible plague epidemic struck Venice and killed some 50,000 people,
a huge part of the population.
Among the victims was the great painter Titian.
In 1576 the doge and the senate made a vow.
If the city were freed from the epidemic they would build a church dedicated to Christ the
Redeemer and every year they would go there in procession.
The design was entrusted to Palladio, who had already designed San Giorgio Maggiore.
The first stone was laid in 1577.
Palladio died in 1580 before the work was finished and the church was completed following
his design.
The building site was directed by Antonio de Ponte, the same architect as the Rialto
Bridge.
The church was consecrated in 1592.
The church was entrusted to the Capuchin friars, a poor and austere order.
That is why, although it was a state monument, the Redentor has a restrained interior,
with almost no lavish decoration.
Look at the façade.
As at San Giorgio, Palladio overlaps two ancient temple fronts,
but here the church is raised on a broad flight of steps,
which makes it even more solemn when seen from the water.
The steps are said to recall those of the temple of Jerusalem.
As you enter you are surrounded by light.
The single, wide nave, with sidechappals, leads the eye towards the high altar and
the dome.
The white walls, the columns and the perfect proportions create an atmosphere of calm and
order.
More than the individual works of art, what matters here is the space.
Palladio himself is the protagonist.
For centuries, every year the Dojan person crossed the canal with the senate and the
authorities, walking over the bridge of boats to the church to attend the solemn mass.
Behind the church the Capuchin friars cultivated a large garden overlooking the
lagoon, which still partly survives and can be visited on certain occasions.
But the redontor is famous above all for its festival.
Every year, on the third Sunday of July, Venetians keep the vow of 1576.
For the occasion, a long boat of bridge of boats and pontoons is built across the
Judeca canal, from the Zatorae to the church.
The most eagerly awaited moment however is Saturday night.
Thousands of Venetians gather on boats decorated with lanterns and balloons,
and along the waterfront, to dine outdoors on traditional dishes,
such as sardae and saur, sweeten saur-sardines.
Around midnight the basin of St Mark lights up with one of the most spectacular
firework displays in Italy, reflected on the water among the boats.
According to an old tradition, after the fireworks the young people head to
the Lido to wait for dawn on the beach.
As you leave, look to the right along the waterfront.
Not far away is another church designed by Palladio, the Zittel.
Together with San Giorgio and the redontor, it forms a classical and harmonious waterfront,
one of the most recognizable landscapes of Venice.
You are in front of the Teatro La Fenice, one of the most famous opera houses in the world.
Its name already tells its story.
The phoenix La Fenice in Italian is the legendary bird that dies in flames and is reborn from its own ashes.
And this theatre has truly been reborn more than once.
At the end of the 18th century, Venice was Europe's capital of theatre.
Dozens of theatres were active in the city and music was part of daily life.
The company of an important theatre, the San Benedetto, lost its home after a legal dispute
and decided to build a new one, more beautiful than all the others.
The design was entrusted to the architect Gianantonio Selva and La Fenice opened in 1792.
The chosen name was already a good omen.
The theatre was to rise again more splendid than before.
Look at the façade on Campo San Fantin.
It is restrained in neoclassical style, very different from the lavish interior.
Above the entrance you can see the image of the phoenix and the Latin word Sosietas,
recalling the society of nobles and citizens who financed the theatre.
At the back, a water entrance allowed spectators to arrive by gondola right inside the theatre.
A few years later, after the fall of the Republic, La Fenice also welcomed Napoleon.
The imperial box was built for him, in the centre of the auditorium, and it still dominates the theatre today.
In 1836 a fire destroyed the interior.
The Venetians rebuilt it in just one year.
It was precisely in that period that La Fenice enjoyed its most glorious season.
Operas by Rossini and Bellini had their premiers here, and above all operas by Giuseppe Verdi,
Anani, Attila, Simon Boconegra, Rigoletto and La Traviata, which was a fiasco at its first performance in 1853.
Today it is one of the most performed operas in the world.
In the 20th century too, La Fenice remained a theatre of important premiers,
such as Igor Stravinsky's The Rake's Progress and Benjamin Britton's The Turn of the Screw.
The most famous voices have sung on its stage, including Maria Callas,
who in 1949 amaze the audience by performing two completely different roles in the same week.
Then, on the night of the 29th of January 1996, the theatre burned once again.
Images of the flames above the rooftops of Venice went around the world.
It turned out that the fire had been started by two electricians working in the theatre,
who were behind schedule with their work.
The city decided to rebuild it as it was and where it was, following 19th century drawings and photographs.
Craftsmen, guilders and restorers worked for years,
and La Fenice reopened in December 2003 with a great concert conducted by Riccardo Muti.
For many Venetians it was like getting back a part of their own home.
If you can, visit the interior.
The auditorium is a triumph of gilded stucco, mirrors and velvet,
with four tiers of boxes and the gallery above arranged in a horseshoe.
Everything was rebuilt with traditional techniques, without forgetting modern safety and acoustics.
Every year, on the 1st of January, the New Year's concert is broadcast on television from La Fenice and heard all over Italy.
It is one of the moments when the theatre reminds everyone of its name,
a phoenix that, after every fire, has always found the strength to be reborn.
